explanation: `git restore --staged` replaces the older `git reset HEAD <file>`.
tip: It is safe: your file edits remain in your editor.
Warning: discarded unstaged changes cannot be recovered by Git!

explanation: Amend replaces the most recent commit with a new hash.
tip: Only amend local commits that haven't been pushed to a shared remote yet.

explanation: Reset moves the timeline backwards; Revert steps forward by recording an inverse commit.
tip: Revert is the gold standard for teamwork.
If you need to save temporary work, use `git stash` instead of resetting.

explanation: Revert preserves history integrity for all collaborators.
tip: You can push a revert commit with regular `git push` without any force flag.

explanation: `git reset --soft` is perfect for combining multiple commits or splitting one.
tip: Your code is still in the staging area ready to re-commit.

explanation: `~` goes back linearly through commit parents.
tip: `HEAD^` and `HEAD~1` refer to the same parent commit in linear history.

explanation: Restores all tracked files to the index state.
tip: Always run `git status` or `git diff` first to see what you are discarding.
Always test with `git clean -n` (dry-run) first to see what would be deleted!
